Equity Research Note — Industrial Automation Sector

Nimbus Robotics, Inc. (NASDAQ: NMBR) vs. Solace Dynamics Corp. (NYSE: SLDC) — Comparative Analysis

Analyst: J. Whitfield, Senior Analyst — Industrial Technology | July 2026

Summary

Summary

Both Nimbus Robotics (NMBR) and Solace Dynamics (SLDC) compete in the collaborative and industrial robotics market. NMBR has posted stronger top-line growth over the trailing four quarters but has seen more pronounced margin compression from input cost inflation. SLDC has grown more slowly but maintained tighter cost discipline and a materially lower leverage profile.

Margin & Profitability Comparison

Margin & Profitability Comparison

NMBR's gross margin fell from 43.7% to 38.2% year-over-year in Q2 2026, driven by steel and semiconductor input cost inflation of roughly 21%. SLDC's gross margin declined more modestly, from 41.0% to 39.1% over the same period, as SLDC had already diversified its component sourcing across three geographies in 2024, reducing its exposure to any single supplier price shock.

Leverage & Liquidity Comparison

SLDC carries substantially lower leverage and higher interest coverage, giving it more balance-sheet flexibility to absorb further input cost shocks without needing to draw additional revolver capacity. NMBR's debt-to-equity ratio rose from 0.94x to 1.23x over the past year specifically because it drew on its revolving credit facility to fund inventory build ahead of anticipated further cost increases — a deliberate but risk-increasing choice, not a result of declining equity value.
Growth & Valuation

NMBR trades at a forward P/E of 18.4x on trailing four-quarter revenue growth of approximately 8.9%. SLDC trades at a forward P/E of 15.1x on trailing four-quarter revenue growth of approximately 5.2%. On a pure growth basis NMBR appears more attractively priced relative to its growth rate, but this does not fully account for NMBR's higher leverage and greater margin volatility — two factors that increase the risk premium a rational investor should apply to NMBR's earnings relative to SLDC's.

Notably, higher revenue growth alone has not translated into higher relative valuation multiples for NMBR versus SLDC on a risk-adjusted basis: NMBR's stock is up only 3% over the trailing twelve months despite faster revenue growth, while SLDC's stock is up 11%, reflecting the market's discounting of NMBR's margin and leverage trajectory.

Recommendation

Recommendation

We rate NMBR Neutral and SLDC Outperform. Investors seeking growth exposure to the robotics sector with lower balance-sheet risk should favor SLDC. NMBR remains a reasonable holding for investors with higher risk tolerance who believe management's supplier-diversification and fixed-price steel contract actions will restore gross margin by fiscal 2027.

Nimbus Robotics, Inc.
Form 10-Q (Excerpt) — Quarterly Report — Period Ended June 30, 2026 — NASDAQ: NMBR
Item 2. Management's Discussion and Analysis of
Financial Condition and Results of Operations
Net revenue for the three months ended June 30, 2026 was $412.6 million, an increase of 9.4%
year-over-year, driven primarily by higher unit shipments of our collaborative robotic arm product line.
Gross margin declined to 38.2%, down from 43.7% in the prior-year period. The decline was driven

primarily by a sustained increase in input costs for steel castings and semiconductor components used in
our servo drive assemblies, which together rose approximately 21% year-over-year, combined with
elevated freight surcharges related to ongoing carrier capacity constraints.
Diluted earnings per share for the quarter were $0.61, down from $0.89 in the prior-year period.
Management estimates that approximately $0.19 of the $0.28 year-over-year EPS decline is directly

attributable to gross margin compression from input cost inflation, with the remainder attributable to higher
interest expense on variable-rate debt and increased R&D; investment in our next-generation
vision-guided picking system.
We have taken several mitigating actions, including qualifying a second semiconductor supplier in
Southeast Asia to reduce single-source exposure, and entering into a 12-month fixed-price agreement for

approximately 60% of our steel casting volume beginning in Q3 2026. Management expects these actions
to partially offset margin pressure beginning in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, though we do not expect
gross margin to return to prior-year levels before fiscal 2027.
Liquidity and Capital Resources
As of June 30, 2026, total debt outstanding was $612.4 million, consisting of $450.0 million in senior notes

and $162.4 million drawn on our revolving credit facility. Total stockholders' equity was $498.1 million,
resulting in a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 1.23x, up from 0.94x at the end of fiscal 2025. The
increase in leverage primarily reflects the additional revolver drawdown used to fund inventory build ahead
of anticipated further input cost increases. Our current ratio at quarter-end was 1.4x, compared to 1.7x a
year ago.
Risk Factors (Updated)

Risk Factors (Updated)
Sustained increases in the cost of steel, semiconductor components, or freight could continue to compress
gross margin faster than we are able to offset through pricing actions or supplier diversification. Our
variable-rate revolving credit facility exposes us to interest rate risk; a 100 basis point increase in reference
rates would increase annualized interest expense by approximately $1.6 million based on the current
outstanding balance.

Nimbus Robotics, Inc. (NASDAQ: NMBR)
Q2 2026 Earnings Call Transcript — July 22, 2026

Operator: Good morning and welcome to the Nimbus Robotics second quarter fiscal 2026 earnings call.
Joining us today are CEO Elena Marsh and CFO David Ochoa.

Elena Marsh, CEO:
Thank you. Q2 was a quarter of contrasts. Revenue grew 9.4% year-over-year to $412.6 million, ahead
of our guidance range, driven by strong demand for our collaborative arm product line, particularly
in automotive and electronics assembly customers. At the same time, we saw meaningful gross margin
pressure from input costs, which I'll let David walk through in detail.

David Ochoa, CFO:
Thanks, Elena. Gross margin came in at 38.2%, down five and a half points year-over-year. The primary
driver was a roughly 21% year-over-year increase in the combined cost of steel castings and
semiconductor components used in our servo drive assemblies. We also saw elevated freight surcharges
tied to ongoing carrier capacity constraints, which added a smaller but still meaningful drag.

Diluted EPS was $0.61 versus $0.89 a year ago. Of that $0.28 decline, we estimate about $0.19 is
directly attributable to gross margin compression from these input costs, with the remaining $0.09
split between higher interest expense on our revolver draw and increased R&D spend on our
next-generation vision-guided picking system.

On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $612.4 million in total debt against $498.1 million
in equity, putting our debt-to-equity ratio at 1.23x, up from 0.94x a year ago. That increase reflects
a deliberate decision to draw on our revolver to build inventory ahead of what we expect to be further
input cost increases in the second half of the year — it is not a reflection of deteriorating
profitability.

We're taking two concrete actions to address the cost pressure. First, we've qualified a second
semiconductor supplier in Southeast Asia to reduce single-source exposure. Second, we've locked in a
12-month fixed-price agreement covering about 60% of our steel casting volume starting in Q3. We
expect these actions to begin offsetting margin pressure in Q4, though we don't expect gross margin
to fully recover to prior-year levels until fiscal 2027.

Analyst Q&A — Marcus Webb, Fairview Capital:
Q: David, can you help us understand why margin didn't recover faster given you've had a couple of
quarters now to react to input cost inflation?
A (Ochoa): The steel and semiconductor cost increases were broader and more sustained than we
initially modeled at the start of the year. We didn't want to lock into a long-term fixed-price
contract until we had better visibility, which is why the fixed-price agreement only starts in Q3.

In hindsight we could have moved faster on supplier diversification, but we prioritized getting the
right long-term partner rather than the fastest option.

Analyst Q&A — Priya Nair, Ashcroft Securities:
Q: Should we read the revolver drawdown as a signal you're worried about further cost increases, and
how are you thinking about leverage going forward?
A (Ochoa): It's fair to say we built inventory defensively. We're comfortable operating up to roughly
1.5x debt-to-equity for a limited period, but we do expect to delever back toward 1.0x by the end of
fiscal 2027 as the fixed-price steel contract and new semiconductor supplier reduce the need for
precautionary inventory build.

Elena Marsh, CEO (closing):
To summarize: strong demand, real cost pressure, and a clear plan to offset it. We're confident in
the actions we've laid out and expect margin trends to inflect in the fourth quarter.

Operator: This concludes today's call.
